'''Jesse Douglas''' (July 3, 1897&nbsp;– September 7, 1965) was an American mathematician and [[Fields Medal]]ist known for his general solution to [[Plateau's problem]].

== Life and career ==
He was born to a [[Jewish]] family<ref>''Peter Lax, Mathematician: An Illustrated Memoir'', by Reuben Hersh
(American Mathematical Soc. 2014), page 102</ref> in [[New York City]], the son of Sarah (née Kommel) and Louis Douglas. He attended [[City College of New York]] as an undergraduate, graduating with honors in Mathematics in 1916.  He then moved to [[Columbia University]] as a graduate student, obtaining a [[PhD]] in mathematics in 1920.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www-history.mcs.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Douglas.html|title=Jesse Douglas (1897–1965)|website=www-history.mcs.st-andrews.ac.uk}}</ref>

Douglas was one of two winners of the first [[Fields Medal]]s,<ref name="Jesse Douglas Biographical Memoir">{{cite web | title=Jesse Douglas (1897–1965): A Biographical Memoir |last1=Colding |first1=Tobias Holck |last2=Minicozzi |first2=William P.| url=https://www.nasonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Douglas_Jesse.pdf | access-date=January 14, 2024}}</ref> awarded in 1936. He was honored for solving, in 1930, the [[Plateau problem|problem of Plateau]], which asks whether a minimal surface exists for a given boundary. The problem, open since 1760 when [[Joseph Louis Lagrange|Lagrange]] raised it, is part of the [[calculus of variations]] and is also known as the ''[[soap bubble]] problem''. Douglas also made significant contributions to the [[inverse problem for Lagrangian mechanics|inverse problem of the calculus of variations]]. The [[American Mathematical Society]] awarded him the [[Bôcher Memorial Prize]] in 1943.

Douglas worked at [[Columbia University]], the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] and the [[Institute for Advanced Study]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Jesse Douglas {{!}} Mathematician, Fields Medalist, Harvard Professor {{!}} Britannica |url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/Jesse-Douglas |access-date=2025-01-01 |website=www.britannica.com |language=en}}</ref> Later he became a full professor at the [[City College of New York]] where he taught until his death. At the time CCNY only offered undergraduate degrees and he taught the advanced calculus course.
